Regression Analysis: Companion R Notebook

Version 0.9

Alexis Diamond, PhD (assisted by Claude and ChatGPT)

August 26, 2026

This notebook accompanies the regression-analysis chapters. Run the chunks in order. All statistical and plotting code uses base R grammar; no tidyverse syntax is required.

Chapter 1: Introducing Regression as a Prediction Machine

Conditional means and a fitted regression

The empirical conditional means show what it means to ask for the expected value of Y at each observed value of X. The fitted line is one rule for generating predictions.

x <- rep(c(1, 2, 3, 4), each = 5)
y <- c(3, 4, 4, 5, 4,
       5, 5, 6, 7, 7,
       7, 8, 8, 9, 8,
       9, 10, 11, 10, 10)

dat <- data.frame(x, y)

tapply(dat$y, dat$x, mean)
##  1  2  3  4 
##  4  6  8 10
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
summary(fit)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = y ~ x, data = dat)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
##  -1.00  -0.25   0.00   0.25   1.00 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   2.0000     0.4082   4.899 0.000116 ***
## x             2.0000     0.1491  13.416 8.21e-11 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.7454 on 18 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.9091, Adjusted R-squared:  0.904 
## F-statistic:   180 on 1 and 18 DF,  p-value: 8.209e-11
plot(
  dat$x,
  dat$y,
  xlab = "X",
  ylab = "Y",
  main = "Observed Outcomes and a Fitted Regression"
)
abline(fit, lwd = 2)

Linear regression and LOESS

Both methods are prediction machines for a conditional mean, but they impose very different amounts of structure.

set.seed(123)

x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 60)
y <- 2 + 0.35 * x + 1.5 * sin(x) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.5)

dat_curve <- data.frame(x, y)

fit_linear <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat_curve)
fit_loess <- loess(y ~ x, data = dat_curve, span = 0.60)

plot(
  dat_curve$x,
  dat_curve$y,
  xlab = "X",
  ylab = "Y",
  main = "Linear Regression and LOESS"
)
abline(fit_linear, lwd = 2)

ord <- order(dat_curve$x)
lines(
  dat_curve$x[ord],
  predict(fit_loess)[ord],
  lwd = 2,
  lty = 2
)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c("Linear regression", "LOESS"),
  lty = c(1, 2),
  lwd = 2,
  bty = "n"
)

Different regression families for different outcomes

The following examples show continuous, binary, count, and flexible conditional-mean models.

set.seed(42)

# Continuous outcome
x_cont <- runif(200, 0, 10)
y_cont <- 4 + 2 * x_cont + rnorm(200, sd = 3)
dat_cont <- data.frame(x = x_cont, y_cont = y_cont)
fit_ols <- lm(y_cont ~ x, data = dat_cont)

# Binary outcome
x_binary <- runif(200, 0, 10)
p_binary <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(-3 + 0.6 * x_binary)))
y_binary <- rbinom(200, size = 1, prob = p_binary)
dat_binary <- data.frame(x = x_binary, y_binary = y_binary)
fit_logit <- glm(
  y_binary ~ x,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = dat_binary
)

# Count outcome
x_count <- runif(200, 0, 5)
lambda <- exp(0.4 + 0.25 * x_count)
count <- rpois(200, lambda = lambda)
dat_count <- data.frame(x = x_count, count = count)
fit_pois <- glm(
  count ~ x,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = dat_count
)

# Flexible conditional-mean smoother
fit_loess <- loess(y ~ x, data = dat_curve)

summary(fit_ols)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = y_cont ~ x, data = dat_cont)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -7.9344 -1.8695  0.0093  1.8318  8.2710 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  3.82928    0.41936   9.131   <2e-16 ***
## x            2.00459    0.07013  28.583   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 2.889 on 198 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.8049, Adjusted R-squared:  0.8039 
## F-statistic:   817 on 1 and 198 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
summary(fit_logit)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = y_binary ~ x, family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
##     data = dat_binary)
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept) -3.39129    0.48103  -7.050 1.79e-12 ***
## x            0.62633    0.08464   7.399 1.37e-13 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 276.28  on 199  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 186.63  on 198  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 190.63
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
summary(fit_pois)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = count ~ x, family = poisson(link = "log"), data = dat_count)
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)  0.41540    0.09398   4.420 9.87e-06 ***
## x            0.23250    0.02872   8.095 5.72e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for poisson family taken to be 1)

## Residual deviance: 196.52  on 198  degrees of freedom

Chapter 2: Technical Foundations of OLS

Binary predictor: coefficient equals the difference in means

D <- c(rep(0, 5), rep(1, 5))
Y <- c(4, 5, 6, 7, 8,
       7, 8, 9, 10, 11)

dat_binary_ols <- data.frame(D, Y)

fit_binary <- lm(Y ~ D, data = dat_binary_ols)
summary(fit_binary)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = Y ~ D, data = dat_binary_ols)
## 
## Residuals:
##    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
##     -2     -1      0      1      2 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)   6.0000     0.7071   8.485 2.85e-05 ***
## D             3.0000     1.0000   3.000   0.0171 *  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 1.581 on 8 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.5294, Adjusted R-squared:  0.4706 
## F-statistic:     9 on 1 and 8 DF,  p-value: 0.01707
coef(fit_binary)
## (Intercept)           D 
##           6           3
mean(dat_binary_ols$Y[dat_binary_ols$D == 0])
## [1] 6
mean(dat_binary_ols$Y[dat_binary_ols$D == 1])
## [1] 9
mean(dat_binary_ols$Y[dat_binary_ols$D == 1]) -
  mean(dat_binary_ols$Y[dat_binary_ols$D == 0])
## [1] 3
plot(
  jitter(dat_binary_ols$D, amount = 0.04),
  dat_binary_ols$Y,
  xaxt = "n",
  xlab = "Binary predictor D",
  ylab = "Outcome Y",
  main = "OLS with a Binary Predictor"
)
axis(1, at = c(0, 1), labels = c("D = 0", "D = 1"))

abline(fit_binary, lwd = 2)
points(
  c(0, 1),
  c(
    mean(dat_binary_ols$Y[dat_binary_ols$D == 0]),
    mean(dat_binary_ols$Y[dat_binary_ols$D == 1])
  ),
  pch = 15,
  cex = 1.5
)

Regression coefficients are literal prediction instructions

fit_cars <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)
summary(fit_cars)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = dist ~ speed, data = cars)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -29.069  -9.525  -2.272   9.215  43.201 
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) -17.5791     6.7584  -2.601   0.0123 *  
## speed         3.9324     0.4155   9.464 1.49e-12 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 15.38 on 48 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.6511, Adjusted R-squared:  0.6438 
## F-statistic: 89.57 on 1 and 48 DF,  p-value: 1.49e-12
coef(fit_cars)
## (Intercept)       speed 
##  -17.579095    3.932409
# Predictions for training observations
train_predictions <- predict(fit_cars)
head(data.frame(
  speed = cars$speed,
  observed_dist = cars$dist,
  predicted_dist = train_predictions
))
##   speed observed_dist predicted_dist
## 1     4             2      -1.849460
## 2     4            10      -1.849460
## 3     7             4       9.947766
## 4     7            22       9.947766
## 5     8            16      13.880175
## 6     9            10      17.812584
# Predictions for new cases
new_cases <- data.frame(speed = c(10, 15, 20))
new_cases$predicted_dist <- predict(
  fit_cars,
  newdata = new_cases
)
new_cases
##   speed predicted_dist
## 1    10       21.74499
## 2    15       41.40704
## 3    20       61.06908
# Reproduce predict() literally from the coefficients
b <- coef(fit_cars)
manual_predictions <- b[1] + b[2] * new_cases$speed
cbind(new_cases, manual_predictions = manual_predictions)
##   speed predicted_dist manual_predictions
## 1    10       21.74499           21.74499
## 2    15       41.40704           41.40704
## 3    20       61.06908           61.06908
plot(
  cars$speed,
  cars$dist,
  xlab = "Speed",
  ylab = "Stopping distance",
  main = "Regression as a Prediction Rule"
)
abline(fit_cars, lwd = 2)
points(
  new_cases$speed,
  new_cases$predicted_dist,
  pch = 15,
  cex = 1.4
)

Coefficient uncertainty: standard errors, p-values, and confidence intervals

confint(fit_cars, level = 0.95)
##                  2.5 %    97.5 %
## (Intercept) -31.167850 -3.990340
## speed         3.096964  4.767853
coef_table <- summary(fit_cars)$coefficients
coef_table
##               Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
## (Intercept) -17.579095  6.7584402 -2.601058 1.231882e-02
## speed         3.932409  0.4155128  9.463990 1.489836e-12
b_speed <- coef_table["speed", "Estimate"]
se_speed <- coef_table["speed", "Std. Error"]

# Approximate 95% confidence interval
b_speed + c(-1, 1) * 2 * se_speed
## [1] 3.101383 4.763434

Mean squared error and R-squared

fit_cars <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)

summary(fit_cars)$r.squared
## [1] 0.6510794
mse_mean_only <- mean(
  (cars$dist - mean(cars$dist))^2
)

mse_model <- mean(
  (cars$dist - predict(fit_cars))^2
)

mse_mean_only
## [1] 650.7796
mse_model
## [1] 227.0704
1 - mse_model / mse_mean_only
## [1] 0.6510794

Chapter 3: Prediction Uncertainty and Multiple Regression

Three different interval targets

fit <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)

# 1. Confidence intervals for regression coefficients
confint(fit)
##                  2.5 %    97.5 %
## (Intercept) -31.167850 -3.990340
## speed         3.096964  4.767853
# 2. Confidence interval for the conditional mean at speed = 15
predict(
  fit,
  newdata = data.frame(speed = 15),
  interval = "confidence"
)
##        fit      lwr      upr
## 1 41.40704 37.02115 45.79292
# 3. Prediction interval for one new observation at speed = 15
predict(
  fit,
  newdata = data.frame(speed = 15),
  interval = "prediction"
)
##        fit      lwr      upr
## 1 41.40704 10.17482 72.63925

Visualizing a coefficient confidence interval

fit <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)

slope <- coef(fit)["speed"]
slope_ci <- confint(fit)["speed", ]

plot(
  1, slope,
  xlim = c(0.5, 1.5),
  ylim = range(c(0, slope_ci)),
  xaxt = "n",
  xlab = "",
  ylab = "Slope coefficient for speed",
  pch = 19
)

segments(
  x0 = 1,
  y0 = slope_ci[1],
  x1 = 1,
  y1 = slope_ci[2],
  lwd = 3
)

points(1, slope, pch = 19)
axis(1, at = 1, labels = "speed")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)

Plot confidence and prediction bands

fit <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)

speed_grid <- data.frame(
  speed = seq(
    from = min(cars$speed),
    to = max(cars$speed),
    length.out = 200
  )
)

conf_band <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = speed_grid,
  interval = "confidence",
  level = 0.95
)

pred_band <- predict(
  fit,
  newdata = speed_grid,
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.95
)

plot(
  cars$speed,
  cars$dist,
  xlab = "Speed",
  ylab = "Stopping distance",
  main = "Confidence and Prediction Intervals"
)

lines(speed_grid$speed, conf_band[, "fit"], lwd = 3)
lines(speed_grid$speed, conf_band[, "lwr"], lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(speed_grid$speed, conf_band[, "upr"], lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(speed_grid$speed, pred_band[, "lwr"], lty = 3, lwd = 2)
lines(speed_grid$speed, pred_band[, "upr"], lty = 3, lwd = 2)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c(
    "Regression line",
    "Confidence interval for mean",
    "Prediction interval for new observation"
  ),
  lty = c(1, 2, 3),
  lwd = c(3, 2, 2),
  bty = "n"
)

The same point prediction sits at the center of both intervals

fit <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)

b <- coef(fit)

# Calculate the prediction literally from the coefficients
manual_prediction <- b[1] + b[2] * 15
manual_prediction
## (Intercept) 
##    41.40704
# Ask predict() for the point prediction
predict(
  fit,
  newdata = data.frame(speed = 15)
)
##        1 
## 41.40704

Multiple regression and holding predictors fixed

fit_simple <- lm(mpg ~ am, data = mtcars)
fit_multiple <- lm(mpg ~ wt + am, data = mtcars)

coef(fit_simple)
## (Intercept)          am 
##   17.147368    7.244939
coef(fit_multiple)
## (Intercept)          wt          am 
## 37.32155131 -5.35281145 -0.02361522
# Two cars with exactly the same weight
same_weight <- data.frame(
  wt = c(3, 3),
  am = c(0, 1)
)

predicted_mpg <- predict(
  fit_multiple,
  newdata = same_weight
)

predicted_mpg
##        1        2 
## 21.26312 21.23950
predicted_mpg[2] - predicted_mpg[1]
##           2 
## -0.02361522
coef(fit_multiple)["am"]
##          am 
## -0.02361522
# Two cars with the same transmission, different weight
same_transmission <- data.frame(
  wt = c(3, 4),
  am = c(0, 0)
)

predicted_mpg <- predict(
  fit_multiple,
  newdata = same_transmission
)

predicted_mpg[2] - predicted_mpg[1]
##         2 
## -5.352811
coef(fit_multiple)["wt"]
##        wt 
## -5.352811
point_type <- ifelse(mtcars$am == 1, 19, 1)

plot(
  mtcars$wt,
  mtcars$mpg,
  pch = point_type,
  xlab = "Weight (1,000 pounds)",
  ylab = "Miles per gallon",
  main = "Multiple Regression: mpg ~ wt + am"
)

b <- coef(fit_multiple)
abline(a = b["(Intercept)"], b = b["wt"], lwd = 3)
abline(
  a = b["(Intercept)"] + b["am"],
  b = b["wt"],
  lwd = 3,
  lty = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Automatic: am = 0", "Manual: am = 1"),
  pch = c(1, 19),
  lty = c(1, 2),
  lwd = c(3, 3),
  bty = "n"
)

Interactions and centering

fit_interaction <- lm(mpg ~ wt * am, data = mtcars)
summary(fit_interaction)

## Call:

## (Intercept)  31.4161     3.0201  10.402 4.00e-11 ***

## Multiple R-squared:  0.833,  Adjusted R-squared:  0.8151 
## F-statistic: 46.57 on 3 and 28 DF,  p-value: 5.209e-11
mtcars_for_example <- mtcars
mtcars_for_example$wt_centered <-
  mtcars_for_example$wt - mean(mtcars_for_example$wt)

fit_interaction_centered <- lm(

Chapter 4: Functional Form, Interactions, Interpolation, and Extrapolation

Functional form

set.seed(9)

x <- seq(1, 10, length.out = 100)
y <- 5 + 2 * x - 0.25 * x^2 + rnorm(100, sd = 1.5)
dat_functional <- data.frame(x, y)

fit_linear <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat_functional)
fit_quadratic <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2), data = dat_functional)
fit_cubic <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2) + I(x^3), data = dat_functional)
fit_logx <- lm(y ~ log(x), data = dat_functional)

summary(fit_linear)$r.squared
## [1] 0.4643643
summary(fit_quadratic)$r.squared
## [1] 0.767135
summary(fit_cubic)$r.squared
## [1] 0.7671361
summary(fit_logx)$r.squared
## [1] 0.2625474

Additive model versus interaction model

fit_interaction <- lm(mpg ~ wt * am, data = mtcars)

plot(
  mtcars$wt,
  mtcars$mpg,
  pch = ifelse(mtcars$am == 0, 1, 19),
  xlab = "Weight (1,000 pounds)",
  ylab = "Miles per gallon",

auto_wt <- seq(
  min(mtcars$wt[mtcars$am == 0]),
  max(mtcars$wt[mtcars$am == 0]),
  length.out = 100
)

manual_wt <- seq(
  min(mtcars$wt[mtcars$am == 1]),
  max(mtcars$wt[mtcars$am == 1]),
  length.out = 100
)

auto_pred <- predict(
  fit_interaction,
  newdata = data.frame(wt = auto_wt, am = 0)
)

manual_pred <- predict(
  fit_interaction,
  newdata = data.frame(wt = manual_wt, am = 1)

lines(auto_wt, auto_pred, lwd = 3)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Automatic", "Manual"),
  pch = c(1, 19),
  lty = c(1, 2),
  lwd = c(3, 3),
  bty = "n"
)

Interpolation across an unsupported interior gap

set.seed(26)

x_left <- runif(35, min = 1, max = 4)
x_right <- runif(35, min = 7, max = 10)
x <- c(x_left, x_right)

y <- c(
  2 + 3 * x_left + rnorm(35, mean = 0, sd = 0.5),
  28 - x_right + rnorm(35, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)
)

gap_data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

fit_linear <- lm(y ~ x, data = gap_data)
fit_quadratic <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2), data = gap_data)

new_point <- data.frame(x = 5.5)
predict(fit_linear, newdata = new_point)
##        1 
## 14.47983
predict(fit_quadratic, newdata = new_point)
##        1 
## 17.90964
x_grid <- seq(1, 10, length.out = 300)
new_grid <- data.frame(x = x_grid)

linear_hat <- predict(fit_linear, newdata = new_grid)
quadratic_hat <- predict(fit_quadratic, newdata = new_grid)

plot(
  gap_data$x,
  gap_data$y,
  xlab = "X",
  ylab = "Y",
  main = "Interpolation Across a Gap in the Training Data",
  pch = 19
)

rect(
  xleft = 4,
  ybottom = par("usr")[3],
  xright = 7,
  ytop = par("usr")[4],
  density = 12,
  angle = 45,
  border = NA
)

points(gap_data$x, gap_data$y, pch = 19)
lines(x_grid, linear_hat, lwd = 3)
lines(x_grid, quadratic_hat, lwd = 3, lty = 2)
abline(v = c(4, 7), lty = 3)

points(
  5.5,
  predict(fit_linear, newdata = data.frame(x = 5.5)),
  pch = 1,
  cex = 1.5,
  lwd = 2
)

points(
  5.5,
  predict(fit_quadratic, newdata = data.frame(x = 5.5)),
  pch = 2,
  cex = 1.5,
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c(
    "Linear fit",
    "Quadratic fit",
    "Gap with no training observations"
  ),
  lty = c(1, 2, NA),
  lwd = c(3, 3, NA),
  fill = c(NA, NA, "black"),
  density = c(0, 0, 35),
  angle = 45,
  border = c(NA, NA, "black"),
  bty = "n"
)

Support in multiple regression: an unequally supported comparison

Automatic cars in mtcars weigh roughly 2.47 to 5.42 thousand pounds; manual cars roughly 1.51 to 3.57. At a weight of 5, the automatic prediction is supported by nearby observations, but the manual prediction is an extrapolation.

fit_interaction <- lm(mpg ~ wt * am, data = mtcars)

predict(
  fit_interaction,
  newdata = data.frame(
    wt = c(5, 5),
    am = c(0, 1)
  )
)
##          1          2 
## 12.4865177  0.8731378
range(mtcars$wt[mtcars$am == 0])
## [1] 2.465 5.424
range(mtcars$wt[mtcars$am == 1])
## [1] 1.513 3.570

Chapter 5: Regression, Overlap, Model Dependence, and Causal Inference

A constructed observational study with limited overlap

The treatment effect in this constructed dataset is exactly 6. Treatment status is strongly related to x, and the untreated outcome function is nonlinear.

x_control <- rep(0:8, each = 3)
x_treated <- rep(5:16, each = 3)

noise_control <- rep(c(-1, 0, 1), times = 9)
noise_treated <- rep(c(-1, 0, 1), times = 12)

Y0_control <- 5 + x_control + 0.4 * x_control^2 + noise_control
Y0_treated <- 5 + x_treated + 0.4 * x_treated^2 + noise_treated

D <- c(
  rep(0, length(x_control)),
  rep(1, length(x_treated))
)

x <- c(x_control, x_treated)
Y <- c(Y0_control, Y0_treated + 6)

causal_dat <- data.frame(Y, D, x)

Model dependence under poor overlap

fit_linear_adjustment <- lm(
  Y ~ D + x,
  data = causal_dat
)

fit_quadratic_adjustment <- lm(
  Y ~ D + x + I(x^2),
  data = causal_dat
)

coef(fit_linear_adjustment)["D"]
##        D 
## 1.190148
coef(fit_quadratic_adjustment)["D"]
## D 
## 6

The two specifications use the same observations but impose different functional forms. The correctly specified quadratic model recovers 6, while the linear adjustment gives a very different answer because the groups have limited overlap.

Restrict to the region of common support

overlap_dat <- causal_dat[
  causal_dat$x >= 5 & causal_dat$x <= 8,
]

fit_linear_overlap <- lm(
  Y ~ D + x,
  data = overlap_dat
)

fit_quadratic_overlap <- lm(
  Y ~ D + x + I(x^2),
  data = overlap_dat
)

coef(fit_linear_overlap)["D"]
## D 
## 6
coef(fit_quadratic_overlap)["D"]
## D 
## 6

In this deliberately clean example, both specifications now return 6 because treated and control outcomes are directly compared at the same x values.

plot(
  causal_dat$x,
  causal_dat$Y,
  pch = ifelse(causal_dat$D == 1, 19, 1),
  xlab = "Confounder X",
  ylab = "Observed outcome Y",
  main = "Limited Overlap in an Observational Study"
)

abline(v = 5, lty = 3)
abline(v = 8, lty = 3)

legend(
  "topleft",
  legend = c("Control", "Treated", "Overlap: X = 5 to 8"),
  pch = c(1, 19, NA),
  lty = c(NA, NA, 3),
  bty = "n"
)

A perfectly balanced randomized-design illustration

This final example represents a perfectly balanced assignment within each value of x: three of six units receive treatment and three receive control. The true treatment effect remains 6. Because treatment and control have the same covariate support and distribution here, the treatment-only regression and two differently specified adjusted regressions all recover the same treatment contrast in this constructed dataset.

x <- rep(0:16, each = 6)
D <- rep(c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1), times = 17)
noise <- rep(c(-1, 0, 1, -1, 0, 1), times = 17)

Y0 <- 5 + x + 0.4 * x^2 + noise
Y <- Y0 + 6 * D

rct_dat <- data.frame(Y, D, x)

# Difference in means = treatment-only OLS coefficient
mean(rct_dat$Y[rct_dat$D == 1]) -
  mean(rct_dat$Y[rct_dat$D == 0])
## [1] 6
fit_rct_simple <- lm(Y ~ D, data = rct_dat)
fit_rct_linear <- lm(Y ~ D + x, data = rct_dat)
fit_rct_quadratic <- lm(Y ~ D + x + I(x^2), data = rct_dat)

coef(fit_rct_simple)["D"]
## D 
## 6
coef(fit_rct_linear)["D"]
## D 
## 6
coef(fit_rct_quadratic)["D"]
## D 
## 6

Suggested experiments for students

These are useful modifications to try after working through the notebook:

  1. Change the values passed to predict() in the cars examples and watch how point predictions change.
  2. Compare confidence and prediction interval widths near the middle and edges of the observed speed range.
  3. Add an irrelevant predictor to an OLS model and verify that training-set R-squared cannot fall.
  4. In the interpolation-gap example, move the gap or make it wider and compare the linear and quadratic predictions.
  5. In the causal-overlap example, gradually shrink the overlap region and watch the treatment coefficient become more sensitive to functional form.
  6. In the mtcars interaction model, predict manual and automatic mileage at the same weights and inspect where those comparisons are supported by actual data.
